1072.title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1072.hook: a mother at a window, watching the road for a daughter who also rides a lion
1072.carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1072.tomorrow: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1072.howItsDone: In Bengal, Durga Puja is kept as both a celebration of the goddess's victory and a homecoming: families welcome Durga as a married daughter visiting her parents, and on the last day the clay images are carried to a river or pond for immersion.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Devi Mahatmya was read whole, ending with two men by a river, each asking the goddess for what he wanted.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA, READ WHOLE.`

segments.voice: A woman stands at a window, watching the road. A year ago her daughter married and moved far up into the mountains, to a husband who smears himself with ash and has no house to speak of. Now autumn is here, and the daughter is coming home for a few days, bringing the children. The mother has been cooking since morning. She is Menaka, queen of the mountains, in songs people sing in Bengal. And the daughter she's waiting for rides a lion. A new stretch begins: five goddesses, met not as titles but as characters.
screen: `A MOTHER AT A WINDOW.` → `A DAUGHTER COMING HOME.` → `THE DAUGHTER RIDES A LION.`

segments.voice: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati. Over the next days this path takes them one at a time, the way you'd get to know people: what they do, who they love, what makes them angry, what they choose. Some Hindus hear all five as faces of one great Goddess, the way the Devi Mahatmya's goddesses walked back into one. Others hold one of them close as their own. This path tells the stories and leaves that to each family. Start with Durga. In the Devi Mahatmya she's the one the gods can't do without. When the buffalo demon has beaten them, their combined radiance becomes her, and each god hands her a weapon. She laughs in battle. She doesn't need rescuing; she is the rescue. But in Bengal, at Durga Puja, she is also somebody's daughter. Tradition there says she is Uma, born to the mountain king and queen, married to Shiva, and once a year she comes home to her parents. Old songs called agamani are sung in her mother's voice: the waiting, the worry, the joy at the gate. When the festival ends, there are songs of farewell as the image is carried to the water, and people say goodbye the way a family says goodbye to a married daughter going back to her husband's house. So one goddess holds two pictures: the warrior with a weapon in every hand, and the girl whose mother has been at the window all morning. Meeting her as a character means letting her be more than one thing.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone strong in your life, and let their strength be there for a few breaths. Then see that same person somewhere soft, at a kitchen table, laughing, being somebody's child, and let both pictures be true. If you pray, bring them before the Goddess in your own words; if you don't, just hold them both ways at once.
Durga. The goddess the gods couldn't do without, and in Bengal's songs, a daughter coming home. The first of five characters. Today's word.

1073.title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1073.hook: the fiercest face of the Goddess, and the devotees who simply call her mother
1073.carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1073.tomorrow: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1073.howItsDone: Devotees in Bengal and beyond worship Kali as Mother, singing Shakta songs to her, including ones attributed to Ramprasad Sen, and the Kali temple at Dakshineswar, where Ramakrishna served, is still a place of daily worship.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Durga: the warrior the gods couldn't do without, and in Bengal's songs, a daughter coming home to a mother at the window.
screen: `DURGA: ONE GODDESS, TWO PICTURES.`

segments.voice: On a kitchen wall in a family home hangs a calendar print. The goddess on it is dark blue, nearly black, her hair wild, her tongue out. She holds a sword, and a garland of severed heads hangs at her neck. A visitor who has never seen her might take a step back. Then the grandmother of the house walks past, touches the frame, and says softly, Ma. Mother. Nothing frightened in it at all. Today's character is Kali, and how both reactions can happen in one kitchen.
screen: `A DARK GODDESS ON THE KITCHEN WALL.` → `A VISITOR STEPS BACK.` → `A GRANDMOTHER SAYS, MA.`

segments.voice: In the Devi Mahatmya, which this path just read, Kali walks onto the page in battle. The Goddess's face goes dark with anger, and from her forehead Kali leaps out: gaunt, fierce, with a sword and a noose, roaring, tearing through the enemy army. There, she is what the Goddess's anger looks like let loose on evil. So far, terrifying. But the stories keep going. In Bengal, poets came who didn't run from her. Tradition remembers Ramprasad Sen, who sang to Kali the way a child talks to a mother: teasing, complaining, sulking, refusing to be sent away. In his songs she's dark and wild, still his mother, and he expects her to answer. Later, in a Kali temple near Kolkata, a priest named Ramakrishna served her image every day. The stories say he spoke to her as Mother, longed to see her, and wept when he couldn't. Visitors found a man who talked about this fearsome goddess the way a small boy talks about his mom. So here is Kali as a character. She isn't tame; nobody in these stories pretends she's gentle, and the sword stays in her hand. And still the people closest to her call her by a child's word for mother. Some devotees put it this way: she is fierce toward what harms her children, and that's exactly why her children aren't afraid of her.
screen: `KALI LEAPS FROM THE GODDESS'S BROW.` · `A POET SINGS TO HER LIKE A CHILD.` · `A PRIEST CALLS HER MOTHER.` · then, large: `FIERCE, AND STILL MA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that frightened you the first time and grew familiar later, a stern teacher, a big dog next door, a hard new job, and let that first step back return for a few breaths. Then let the second look come, the one that came with knowing it, and notice what changed: the thing, or the one looking. If you pray, say Ma or the Goddess's name quietly, the way the grandmother did; if not, rest with the second look.
Durga. The name over this whole stretch, and the Goddess from whose brow, in the Devi Mahatmya, Kali leaps out. Today's word.

1074.title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1074.hook: a goddess dancing after battle who can't stop, and a god who lies down in her path
1074.carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1074.tomorrow: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1074.howItsDone: In Bengal and elsewhere, images of Kali standing on Shiva, her tongue out, are found in temples and homes, and devotees read the scene both as a family story and as a picture of stillness and power together.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kali, leaping from the brow of Durga's battle-form, and the poet and the priest who still called her Ma.
screen: `KALI: FIERCE, AND STILL MA.`

segments.voice: The battle is over, the demons gone, and Kali is still dancing. In the story people tell, she can't come down from it. Her feet pound the ground until it cracks. The worlds shake. The gods, cheering a moment ago, look at one another in alarm. Who will stop her? Nobody wants to walk up to Kali mid-dance and tap her on the shoulder. Then one of them has an idea, and it isn't a fight. It's an odd move, and it's the scene behind images of Kali standing on someone.
screen: `THE BATTLE IS OVER.` → `KALI IS STILL DANCING.` → `THE WORLDS START TO SHAKE.`

segments.voice: The gods go to Shiva. He doesn't pick up a weapon or argue with her. He walks onto the battlefield and lies down among the fallen, right in her path. Kali, dancing blind, steps on him, looks down, and sees who it is: her own husband, under her foot. In one Bengali telling, that's when her tongue comes out, the way someone bites their tongue in shock: oh no, what have I done. And the dance stops. This story isn't in the Devi Mahatmya. It grew up around Kali afterward, and it's told more than one way. Some tellings say Shiva lay down to calm her; some, so she'd recognize him. The point isn't that he beat her. Nobody beats Kali. He stopped her by being still, and by being someone she loves. Some devotees and teachers read the picture more deeply. Shiva lying there, motionless and pale, is stillness. Kali, dark and moving, is power, energy, everything that happens. The image puts them together on purpose: the dance needs the ground, and the ground on its own doesn't dance. Others simply love it as a family story: a wife so caught up she didn't see her husband, and the look on her face when she did. Either way, the character comes through. Kali's fierceness is real, and it stops for love.
screen: `SHIVA LIES DOWN IN HER PATH.` · `SHE STEPS ON HIM, AND SEES HIM.` · `A STORY TOLD MORE THAN ONE WAY.` · then, large: `STOPPED BY STILLNESS, AND BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit, or lie down if you can, and let the body be completely still, the way Shiva was, while the breath, the heartbeat, racing thoughts and sounds outside keep moving. Don't stop any of it; be the still ground it moves over, and if one thought keeps dancing, let it dance. If you pray, rest in the Goddess's presence; if you don't, rest in the stillness.
Durga. The name over this stretch of five characters, and today, the goddess whose fierce form, as Kali, dances until stillness stops her. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters. Tomorrow, Lakshmi, and the day she left. Rest well.

1075.title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1075.hook: a garland tossed to an elephant, and the goddess of fortune leaves the worlds
1075.carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1075.tomorrow: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1075.howItsDone: Hindus honor Lakshmi in homes and shops, especially at Diwali, and some families keep the house clean and lamps lit in the hope that she will feel welcome and stay.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SEVENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Durga's fierce form as Kali danced until Shiva lay still in her path, and her fierceness stopped for love. Today, a quieter goddess.
screen: `KALI, STOPPED BY STILLNESS.`

segments.voice: Indra, king of the gods, rides his great white elephant, pleased with himself. On the road he meets the sage Durvasa, known for his temper, wandering in a wild, ecstatic state with a garland of heavenly flowers on his own head. Durvasa takes it off and throws it up to the king. Indra catches it and, without really looking, hangs it on the elephant's head. The elephant smells the flowers, takes the garland in its trunk, and throws it on the ground. That careless moment is where Lakshmi's story begins: the day she left.
screen: `A SAGE OFFERS A GARLAND.` → `THE KING HANDS IT TO HIS ELEPHANT.` → `THE GARLAND HITS THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: The sage sees his garland in the dirt, and his temper breaks. In the Vishnu Purana's telling, he curses Indra: since the king is so swollen with his fortune, his fortune will leave him. And it does. Shri, the goddess of fortune and prosperity, also called Lakshmi, departs from the three worlds. What follows is quietly frightening. Nobody attacks; nothing explodes. Things just go dim. In the Purana's description, the plants wither, people stop offering and giving, the gods lose their strength, and the demons start winning. All because one goddess is gone. So who is Lakshmi as a character? Not a warrior like Durga, not wild like Kali. She is the goddess of everything going well: the full granary, the lamp lit, the house where people are generous. In the text her leaving is the sage's curse at work, but some retellers draw a trait from it: she doesn't stay where she isn't honored. She isn't cruel about it. She simply isn't there anymore, and suddenly everyone notices what she was holding together. Some teachers draw a plain lesson: fortune follows care, and slips away from arrogance. A gift tossed aside, a blessing taken for granted, and the shine goes out of things. The story doesn't end in the dark. To bring her back, the gods will have to do something enormous, together with their enemies. That's tomorrow.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one good thing you've stopped noticing, a friend who always texts back, a body that works, a warm room, something you'd only miss if it were gone. Hold it the way Indra should have held the garland, really looking, and let a little gratitude rise without forcing it. If you pray, offer thanks to Lakshmi or to God; if you don't, just notice.
Durga. The name over this run of five goddesses; today, the run turns to Lakshmi, whose leaving dims the worlds. Today's word.

1076.title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1076.hook: Lakshmi rises from the churned ocean holding a garland, and looks over every suitor before she chooses
1076.carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1076.tomorrow: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
1076.howItsDone: Lakshmi is shown seated or standing on a lotus, often beside Vishnu, and Hindus honor her at home and in temples, especially on the night of Lakshmi puja at Diwali.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, in this run under Durga's name, a garland hit the dirt, a sage's curse fell, and Lakshmi left the worlds, and everything went dim.
screen: `THE DAY LAKSHMI LEFT.`

segments.voice: The worlds are dim, and the gods are losing. So they make a truce with their enemies, and together gods and demons churn the ocean of milk, a mountain for the churning stick and a great serpent for the rope, pulling back and forth like a cosmic tug of war. Strange things come up out of the foam. Then, standing on a lotus, holding a lotus, radiant, the goddess herself rises from the waves. Every god and every demon on that shore wants her. Today Lakshmi comes back, and gets to choose.
screen: `GODS AND DEMONS CHURN THE OCEAN.` → `STRANGE THINGS COME UP.` → `LAKSHMI RISES ON A LOTUS.`

segments.voice: In the Vishnu Purana the moment is pure celebration. The rivers come to bathe her, the ocean gives her a garland of unfading flowers, the gods sing her praises, and she goes straight to Vishnu and rests on his chest, and the worlds brighten again. But the Bhagavata Purana slows the moment down and gives Lakshmi a long look. Garland in hand, she walks along the line of suitors, studying them, and finds something missing in each. One has great austerity but hasn't conquered anger. One has knowledge but can't let go of attachment. One is mighty but can't master desire. One is generous, another devoted to duty, and still each falls short somewhere. Then she comes to Vishnu, the one who isn't reaching for her at all, and places the garland on him. That's the character in one scene. Lakshmi isn't a prize handed to the winner; nobody wins her by pulling hardest on the rope. She looks, she weighs, she chooses. Having chosen, tradition says, she stays at his side and goes with him when he comes into the world: some tell of her as Sita beside Rama, and as Rukmini beside Krishna. Yesterday she left where she wasn't honored. Today she chooses where she'll stay. Put together, Lakshmi stops looking like luck that just happens. She looks like someone with judgment, and fortune follows her choices.
screen: `THE OCEAN GIVES HER A GARLAND.` · `SHE STUDIES EVERY SUITOR.` · `EACH FALLS SHORT SOMEWHERE.` · then, large: `SHE LOOKS, SHE WEIGHS, SHE CHOOSES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one choice in front of you, small or large, and don't decide yet: look down the line the way Lakshmi did, one option at a time, noticing what each is missing, without grabbing the loudest. Then let it rest; some choices come clear only after a long look. If you pray, ask for good judgment in your own words; if you don't, just keep looking.
Durga. The name this run of five goddesses sits under; today it belongs to Lakshmi, rising from the ocean, garland in hand. Today's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in this run of Durga and her sister goddesses, Lakshmi rose from the churned ocean, looked down the line of suitors, and chose.
screen: `LAKSHMI: SHE LOOKS, SHE CHOOSES.`

segments.voice: Where does a goddess of learning come from? The familiar image is calm and bright: a woman in white, seated by water, a veena in her hands, a book, a string of beads, a swan nearby. Some students bow to her before exams; some musicians touch her picture before they play. But in the Rig Veda her story isn't a woman with a book at all. It's water, moving fast, carving through hills. Today's character is Saraswati, and she starts out as a river.
screen: `A GODDESS IN WHITE WITH A VEENA.` → `SOME STUDENTS BOW BEFORE EXAMS.` → `BUT FIRST, A RIVER.`

segments.voice: In the Rig Veda, Sarasvati is a river, and the hymns don't treat her as a gentle one. One hymn has her bursting through the ridges of the hills with her strong waves, the way someone digging pulls up lotus roots. She's loud, she's powerful, and she nourishes the people along her banks. One verse gives her a triple praise that's hard to forget: best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses. In Sanskrit it rings: ambitame, naditame, devitame. Mother, river, goddess, in one breath. Over the long life of the tradition, the river becomes the goddess of speech, learning, music and wisdom. Some later texts link her with Vak, sacred speech itself. So the one who flowed now flows another way: through words, through a song, through a mind finally understanding something. Tradition also says the river didn't simply vanish. Pilgrims at Prayag, where the Ganga and the Yamuna meet, speak of a third river joining them there, hidden underground: Sarasvati, unseen but present. So who is Saraswati as a character? The one you can't see, moving under everything: a powerful current that became the flow of knowledge. Some students say learning works the same way: hidden for a long time, and then, suddenly, it surfaces.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you're learning slowly, a language, an instrument, a skill at work, and notice that most of the learning happens where you can't see it; let that be all right. Then just listen, to sounds near and far, and let them flow past like water. If you pray, bow inwardly to Saraswati; if you don't, bow to what you're learning.

1078.howItsDone: Saraswati is invoked as the goddess of speech and learning; some Hindus offer her a short prayer before study, speaking, or performance, and the story of Kumbhakarna's boon is told in Ramayana retellings and plays.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, in this run of Durga and the goddesses, Saraswati began as a rushing river in the Rig Veda and became the flow of learning, unseen and still flowing.
screen: `SARASWATI: UNSEEN, AND STILL FLOWING.`

segments.voice: Three brothers have done fierce austerities for a very long time: Ravana, Vibhishana, and the giant Kumbhakarna. Brahma, the creator, is pleased, and about to grant each a boon. The gods are worried. Ravana's request is bad enough, but Kumbhakarna is enormous and hungry, and whatever he asks for, the worlds may not survive it. So the gods bring Brahma a quiet plea: do something before the giant opens his mouth. This path met this scene once from Kumbhakarna's side. Today, the side of the goddess who walks into it.
screen: `THREE BROTHERS, THREE BOONS.` → `THE GODS FEAR THE GIANT'S WISH.` → `DO SOMETHING BEFORE HE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: In the Uttara Kanda of Valmiki's Ramayana, Brahma calls Saraswati to mind, and she's there beside him. He asks her to go and be the speech in the giant's mouth. She enters Kumbhakarna's speech, and when Brahma asks what he wants, out comes a wish to sleep, for years and years. Brahma grants it. Then the goddess leaves him, and Kumbhakarna, himself again, realizes what he's said, and is dismayed. Look at who Saraswati is here. She doesn't fight, argue, or need a weapon. She is speech itself, and she knows a single wish said out loud can change the shape of the world. Later tellers sharpened it into a pun: he meant to ask for Indra's throne, and the word slipped and became sleep. That pun isn't Valmiki's, but you can see why people loved it: one sound out of place, and history turns. It's a little unsettling, too, the goddess of learning used to trip a tongue. Some readers take it as a warning about how much power our words carry. Others see her protecting the worlds the only way speech can. And with that, the week closes. Durga, the warrior who is also a daughter coming home. Kali, fierce and still called Ma, stopped mid-dance by stillness and love. Lakshmi, who leaves where she isn't honored, then looks long before she chooses. Saraswati, the river underground and the voice in a giant's mouth. One goddess still waits her turn: Parvati.

See the small gap between the thought and the mouth, and how much can happen in it. If you pray, ask Saraswati to guard your speech; if you don't, rest in the gap.
